hero.h0: Finished in March. Still not published.
hero.d0: Good writing stalls between the draft and the place it should be published, or goes out sounding like somebody else.
hero.titleQuestion: What is the piece called? A working title will do.
hero.askQuestion: Tell me the piece in one sentence, the way you’d describe it to a friend at lunch.
hero.askQuestionTitled: Tell me “{title}” in one sentence, the way you’d describe it to a friend at lunch.
hero.askPlaceholder: A guide to keeping bees on a city rooftop, for people who rent.
hero.askNote: Twyne carries on from your answer and asks what it still needs for the brief.

problem.title: The writing was done. Getting it out was not.
problem.lede: The draft is the part people plan for. A finished piece stalls in the hand-offs: from the doc to the editor, from the editor to the style guide, from the style guide to wherever the piece is meant to live.
problem.slip1Body: Final, final v7. Comments from three people, none of them resolved.
problem.slip2Body: A PDF from two years ago. It says “wetland”. The draft says “swamp”.
problem.slip3Body: Pasted into the CMS. Headings lost, links broken, posted under the wrong name.
problem.slip4Body: Trim size, bleed, spine width, keywords. The manuscript waits while its author learns a printer’s vocabulary.
problem.caseBody: Marsh Lane Land Trust has four people and three publications. June drafts a notice that the boardwalk reopens on December 6. Tomás marks it up from his memory of the style guide. Sam copies it into the website by hand. It goes out a day late, with the trust’s name spelled “Marshlane”.
problem.caseNote: Marsh Lane is fictional. You can follow it through Twyne in the walkthroughs below.

turn.title: One desk for the whole journey.
turn.lede: Twyne began as a draft room full of editors. It is becoming the place a piece travels from its first answer to published work, with the same brief, the same house rules and the same editors at every step.
turn.ledgerLabel: The journey, and what you can use today
turn.s1Body: A ten-minute interview becomes the brief every tool reads.
turn.s2Body: Five editors, a rubric and a citation desk read each draft against that brief.
turn.s3Body: Publish a link on Twyne, a standard.site record in your own ATProto repository, or a post to a Micropub site.
turn.s4Body: Voice, terms and banned phrases, written once and checked before anything goes out.
turn.s5Body: Authors ask for review, editors approve, publishers publish.
turn.s6Body: Your address and your look, with feeds and a standard.site proof that the publication is yours.
turn.s7Body: Test readers through VoxQ, then a KDP package or a submission kit for agents.
turn.filmNote: Step into the room as it is today: one minute, with captions.

audiences.title: Three kinds of writer, one desk.
audiences.a1Body: Start from a brief, draft with editors who argue with you, and share the piece as a Twyne link or in your own ATProto repository. Publishing on your own domain, in your own voice, comes next.
audiences.a2Body: One style book for the whole organization. Each piece is checked against it, approved by an editor and released by a publisher on your own domain, in your own look.
audiences.a3Body: Freeze a manuscript, learn where test readers got confused, and leave with a KDP package or a submission kit. Twyne prepares the files; you upload and send them yourself.

walk.title: Follow three pieces from draft to published work.
walk.lede: Three examples, one step at a time. The buttons inside each screen work.
walk.note: Example screens from Twyne Publishing, which is in development. The people are fictional, and nothing you do here is saved or sent.

fieldnote.tabSub: From an app builder to a blog
fieldnote.s1Title: Arrive with the blog already set up
fieldnote.s1Body: Maya built Fieldnote in the Not Organic app builder and published one post there. Twyne opens on the same account with the app, the blog at fieldnote.app/blog, the verified address and that first post carried over. She can untick anything she does not want brought across.
fieldnote.s2Title: Write the second post from a template
fieldnote.s2Body: Fieldnote Journal sits beside her drafts. The voice she chose in the builder, Plain Speaker, arrives as a draft rule. Nothing is checked against it until she switches it on.
fieldnote.s3Title: Fix what breaks the house style
fieldnote.s3Body: The release check names the rule and the passage for each finding. A must-fix finding holds the post back until it is fixed or kept on purpose. Try the buttons: the passage, the count and the Publish button change together.
fieldnote.s4Body: The release sheet shows the page as readers will see it, its address, the feed and whether reader apps may list it. Twyne checks the live page before it calls the post published.

marsh.tabSub: House style, review and a domain
marsh.s1Title: Learn the style from what is already published
marsh.s1Body: Tomás, the trust’s editor, asks Twyne to read up to ten published pieces. It proposes rules, each with an example from the trust’s own writing. Nothing is switched on until he accepts it.
marsh.s2Body: June’s notice passed the release check. Tomás sees the revision, the rules it was checked against and where it will go, then approves it or asks for changes. Editing an approved piece needs a fresh approval.
marsh.s3Body: Sam, the publisher, sees what is approved and waiting, each publication’s address, and which style book version it uses. A different accent colour on Press is flagged, in case it is not on purpose.
marsh.s4Body: Connecting a domain is four separate checks, each with its own fix: the trust controls the domain, HTTPS works, the pages reach Twyne, and the standard.site proof matches.

orchard.tabSub: A novel, test readers and KDP
orchard.s1Title: Check the book is ready for readers
orchard.s1Body: Ines marks her 24 chapters as a book. Twyne lists what is worth a look before anyone reads it: chapter order, length against her target, a name spelled two ways, open margin notes. None of it stops her.
orchard.s2Body: She chooses the questions and who reads: people she invites, a paid panel through Prolific, or both. VoxQ runs the study. Readers see the excerpts she approves inside each question.
orchard.s3Title: Answers come back to the margin
orchard.s3Body: When the study closes, answers arrive as margin notes on the passages readers quoted, with how many said so and how many answered. Simulated pilot answers are kept apart and never counted as readers.
orchard.s4Body: Twyne builds the print PDF, the cover template, the EPUB and a sheet of details to paste. Ines uploads to KDP herself and tells Twyne when the book is submitted. A submission kit for agents is the other route.

room.title: The room, working
room.lede: Click around a copy of the editing room. Every stop on this tour is part of Twyne you can use now.
room.platesTitle: How a piece moves through the room
room.p1Body: Ten minutes of questions about audience, purpose, and what good looks like. The interview becomes a project brief that every tool in the room reads, so no draft starts from a blank page.
room.p2Body: A serious long-form editor with saved drafts and focus tools. Your work stays on your machine, organized into folios you can return to between sessions.
room.p3Body: The Skeptic, the Gentle Reader, the Line Editor, the Critic: each persona marks up the draft in the margin while a rubric grades thesis, structure, style, and evidence against the brief.
room.p4Body: Twyne detects URLs, DOIs, ISBNs, and footnotes as you cite them, and keeps every source in one place where it can be inspected and verified.

close.title: The room is open.
close.body: Start with the interview today. Publishing is being built into the same desk you write in, not as a separate app.
